The Fuel System Monitor reviews how the fuel control system increases or trims flow to compensate for the fuel system components\' normal wearing and aging. This system looks at the fuel system pressure control, injection quantity, injection timing, and feedback control. There are two types of fuel adjustments; Short Term Fuel Trim (STFT), and Long Term Fuel Trim (LTFT). The Powertrain Control Module (PCM) uses the sum of both of these trims to calculate the total fuel correction.

The Comprehensive Component Monitor (CCM) runs to detect failed engine and transmission, sensor or actuator, inputs and outputs that aren\'t tested by other monitors. This monitor checks for any shorts, opens, out of range, or irrational values in comparison to powertrain data tables (predetermined by manufacturer). The CCM specifically monitors for malfunctions in any powertrain electronic component or circuit that provide input or output signals to the Powertrain Control Module (PCM). This will probably be one of the monitors that trigger the check engine light most often.

The catalyst holds the key to a vehicle\'s ability to comply with smog checks. The catalytic converter converts harmful emissions to harmless gases and water. This is the heart of the OBD 2 since the OBD 2 was originally designed to measure emissions levels. The catalyst oxidizes the exhaust when the oxygen content of the exhaust is low. The addition of a second O2 sensor located after the catalytic output helps determine the catalyst efficiency.

The catalyst is used to convert harmful emissions leaving the exhaust manifold to harmless gases and water. A heated catalyst is a catalyst with an electrical heater. This heater helps a cold catalyst warm up to an optimized operating temperature at a faster rate so it can start working sooner. This results in a quicker response to reduction of harmful emissions.

The Evaporative Emissions Control System (EVAP) monitor is used to ensure that the fuel storage and vapor recovery systems remain intact and functional throughout the vehicle\'s life. In other words, this monitor is used to prevent gas from escaping from the fuel tank and fuel system. Fuel tends to expand when heated, and preventing these pressurized fuel vapors from escaping into the environment is not an easy task.

The secondary air system, also known as the air injection system, is a system designed to add extra oxygen to the exhaust stream. The purpose is to help reduce the number of excess hydrocarbons in the exhaust before reaching the catalytic converter. This will help reduce exhaust emissions and pollutants into the environment. The monitor reviews the components, switches, and solenoids that are part of the air injection system.

Automotive air conditioning is used to cool and remove humidity from the air inside the vehicle to meet the air quality specified by the driver or passenger. There are three main parts to the system: the compressor, condenser and evaporator. A refrigerant (refrigerant R-134a) runs through these components and changes phases (liquid and gas) as heat is transferred from one location to another. This monitor ensures that if the vehicle were to run at worse case scenario when the A/C compressor is running 24 hours a day, it would still meet emission standards.

The Oxygen (O2) sensor sets the emission limits on the vehicle. The O2 sensors are located on the exhaust manifold and are used to monitor the amount of unburned oxygen in the exhaust stream when the fuel mixture exits the engine. This requires the O2 sensor to be in tip top shape. When the car computer runs tests, the O2 sensors become one of the most important parameters. These sensors are required to respond quickly and accurately.

The oxygen sensor heater is used with the oxygen sensor to allow the Powertrain Control Module (PCM) to switchover from open loop to closed loop operation. The purpose of the heater is to heat up the sensor so that the switchover can occur as soon as possible after the engine startup. Once the oxygen sensor can produce a useable signal after a specified time after startup, then the oxygen sensor heater monitor will be satisfied. Some OBD-II systems perform an active test to check the oxygen sensor heater directly, while others indirectly check with deductive tests.

Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) is an emissions reduction technique used in both petrol/gas and diesel engines. It is the process in internal combustion engines where exhaust gas is delicately added in a precise amount to the combustion chamber (engine cylinders) at a particular time. This decreases the amount of O2 in the incoming airstream and also provides gases to help reduce peak in-cylinder temperatures. The EGR monitor attempts to control the NOx emissions.
The Non-Methane HydroCarbon (NMHC) catalyst monitor is used to ensure that there is a proper conversion of hydrocarbons and carbon monoxides to meet emission limits.

Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) is an advanced emission controlling system used to decrease the amount of Nitrogen Oxide (NOx) into the environment. This system injects a liquid reductant urea solution known as Diesel Exhaust Fluid (DEF) through a special catalyst into the exhaust stream. It is a means of converting Nitrogen Oxide (NOx) into diatomic nitrogen (N2) to help aid the catalyst. A car equipped with this will have many advantages including extremely low emissions, low fuel consumption, and reduced emissions of oxides of nitrogen.

The Boost Pressure System is used to increase the pressure inside the intake manifold to a level greater than atmospheric pressure. The increased pressure helps ensure combustion of the air-fuel mixture takes place. The Boost Pressure Monitor tests for component integrity, system operation, and faults.
The Exhaust Gas Sensors are used in several systems and monitors to determine the content of the exhaust stream.

Diesel cars are equipped with Diesel Particulate Filters (DPFs). These filters physically trap and remove particulate matter (PM) from the engine\'s exhaust. The filters are self-cleaning. The system periodically modifies the exhaust gas concentration to burn off trapped particles in the honeycomb-structured filter. So, the DPF collects a lot of PM and eventually the passage may become blocked. This causes an increase in exhaust backpressure. When the filter element reaches a temperature required for the combustion of the accumulated PM, it converts the PM to ash, CO2 and water.

Monitors are groups of sensors that perform and coordinate test exercises. These monitor tests ultimately turn the Malfunction Indicator Light (MIL), also known as check engine light, on or off. Monitors set Diagnostic Trouble Codes (DTCs), and can self-erase them. All monitors have requirements known as ENABLING CRITERIA, which differ for each monitor and can range from sensors meeting a particular condition, to the completion of other monitors. Once a monitor has achieved its enabling criteria, the monitor will run tests to check for synchronism and responsiveness between specific sensors in the vehicle. It is important to remember that although all cars have similar monitors, each monitor goes through a carefully selected experiment, comparing information from several sensors to see if the information is logical and complete. Some monitors run continuously, while others run only once when the ENABLING CRITERIA are satisfied. All monitors have to run completely to have comprehensive results and a way to ensure this is to take the car for a TRIP ( test ride ).

The Powertrain Control Module (PCM) uses specified tests, known as monitors, to determine if all sensors in a subsystem operate properly and produce acceptable emissions solution. The tests are used as rationality checks. For each monitor, ENABLING CRITERIA must be met during a TRIP before the PCM can successfully run that monitor.
A monitor TRIP is when the vehicle goes through the following series of events:
2) The engine meets the specific monitor\'s ENABLING CRITERIA.

TRIPS vary with each monitor since each monitor has different ENABLING CRITERIA. Some FAULTS will turn the Malfunctioning Indicator Light (MIL), on in one trip while others in two (depending on the specific monitor). This property is defined as ONE-TRIP or TWO-TRIP monitors. As soon as the MIL is requested on, a TRIP COUNTER is started. This keeps track of how many trips are made after the fault is recorded. If the PCM doesn\'t detect a fault in the next three trips, the MIL is turned off. If the enabling criteria cannot be repeated for whatever reason then the MIL will remain on.
There are two types of monitors:

CONTINUOUS monitors run when the enabling criteria for the monitor are met, the monitor continues to run and constantly reviews the systems for a component fault (either electrical or logical). There are three continuous monitors: Comprehensive Component Monitor, Misfire Detection Monitor, and Fuel System Monitor. These monitors hold the responsibility of flagging any major issues that may cause direct problems to the catalytic converter (please refer the descriptions for these monitors more information).

NON-CONTINUOUS monitors run when the enabling criteria are met, they perform and complete their testing once per trip. The NON-CONTINUOUS monitors are different for spark ignition (gasoline engines) and compression ignition (diesel engines) vehicles.
There are 3 different ways monitors can perform tests:

A PASSIVE test is when the monitors\' sensors for rationality and out of range responses. This is used to detect obvious faults like open or short circuits. For instance, if the throttle position sensor is reading a closed position and the mass airflow sensor is reading a high airflow, then one of these sensors is reading an incorrect value (since a closed throttle should read a little to no airflow).

An ACTIVE test is normally in response to a failed passive test. The PCM takes direct control of the component to determine its functionality. It may command a component to do something and check if it responds to the command."

An INTRUSIVE test is similar to an active test. The PCM takes control of a component but what makes it intrusive is that the test can have an effect on vehicle performance or emissions levels. For instance, the PCM may command a valve open when it’s normally supposed to be closed just to see if it responds to command.

When a fault occurs, a FREEZE FRAME is stored. Typical freeze frame data include many vehicle parameters. For instance, calculated engine load (in percent), engine revs (in RPM), short and long term fuel trim (in percent), fuel pressure (if available) and vehicle speed. The freeze frame will also store the DTC that caused the fault. If the code is related to a misfire, the offending cylinder may be identified as well.

The monitors use a task manager or \'diagnostic execute\' to manage operations of monitors and keep them from affecting vehicle performance. The task manager also makes sure that the monitors runtime is in proper sequential order, and prevents potential conflicts between individual monitors. Before running each monitor, the task manager ensures the operating conditions are met, and the required prerequisite monitors (if applicable) have ran and completed.
The task manager makes priorities amongst the monitors by establishing one of the following statuses:

PENDING is when the task manager must wait for other monitors/sensors before executing. For instance, if there is a failed sensor needed for a monitor to run, the task manager will be pending for a repair before running.

CONFLICT is when a monitor cannot complete its tests due to other monitors current operation, or incorrect and missing information. For instance, two monitors are trying to run at the same time, this will cause a conflict. Some monitors manipulate the same sensors for their individual tests, so this can cause conflicting issues.

SUSPEND is when a monitor stops because there is insufficient information. If for instance, Monitor A is required to complete before Monitor B can run, then the task manager will suspend Monitor B until Monitor A is complete
This is a lot to absorb. Just remember that if your application is showing for instance the misfire is not complete, it may just be that the proper requirements have not been met yet.
This process is as a generic OBD II Drive Cycle Guide:
Step 1: Ensure there is no check engine light currently on (look at your dashboard)
Step 2: Connect the device and check monitor status and precondition.
Step 3: Ensure fuel tank is between 1/4 and 3/4 full.
Step 4: Start engine at cold temperatures (less than 86 F) and warm up until engine coolant temp is at least 160 F.
Step 5: Speed up to 40-60 mph at 25% throttle (maintain for 5 minutes)
Step 6: Ensure engine coolant temperature reaches and stays above 190 F.
Step 7: Slow down without using the break to 20 mph (or less).
Step 8: Stop vehicle and allow it to idle for 10 seconds.
Step 9: Turn key off, wait 2 minutes to power down PCM
Step 10: Turn on the car and repeat steps 5 through 9.

A misfiring cylinder is defined as a situation when the air-fuel mixture fed into the cylinder fails to ignite. There are three basic reasons why a continuous misfire would occur: loss of spark (spark plugs), the air/fuel mix ratio is too far out of range to ignite, or there is a loss in compression. When misfires occur the engine performance suffers significantly, along with fuel economy, emissions, and idle quality. This monitor is strictly used to detect continuous misfires through the use of the Crankshaft Position (CKP) device.
